content.text: Eddy currents are a major source of energy loss in an iron core transformer.
What is one way to minimise this energy loss?
Laminate the iron core with an insulator
Put fewer turns of wire in the primary coil
Operate the transformer with a higher current
Decrease the distance between the primary and secondary coils

Think about how the paths available to those currents could be interrupted without changing the material of the core.

I. Extreme heat
II. Weightlessness
III. Communication blackout
Which combination of these conditions is associated with safe re-entry of a manned spacecraft?
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only

Weightlessness is a consequence of the spacecraft being in free fall in orbit, not of re-entry, so one of the three listed conditions is not a re-entry hazard at all.
B

During re-entry the spacecraft moves rapidly through the atmosphere. Air resistance converts kinetic energy into thermal energy, so extreme heat is a genuine hazard that must be managed. content.text: Why did the Braggs use X-rays to determine the crystal structure of metals?
X-rays have a low frequency.
X-rays have a short wavelength.
X-rays can pass through metals.
X-rays travel at the speed of light.

Diffraction is only strong when the wavelength of the wave is comparable to the distance between the objects producing the pattern. Compare the wavelength of X-rays with the spacing of the atoms in a crystal lattice.
Being able to pass through a metal, or travelling at the speed of light, tells you nothing about the size of the features that can be resolved.
B

Diffraction is only significant when the wavelength is comparable to the spacing between the diffracting objects. Atomic spacings in a crystal are of the order of $10^{-10}$ m, which is comparable to the wavelength of X-rays, so X-rays produce a strong diffraction pattern from the crystal lattice. Their speed and ability to pass through metals are irrelevant to resolving the lattice spacing. Option B.

content.text: Why is a magnet able to hover above a superconductor that is below its critical temperature?
The superconductor excludes magnetic flux.
The superconductor loses conductive properties when placed in a magnetic field.
The eddy current in the superconductor creates a potential difference between the magnet and the superconductor.
The gravitational force on the magnet is balanced by the force created by the crystal lattice structure of the superconductor.
Consider what happens to a magnetic field inside a material cooled below its critical temperature: this is the effect named after Meissner.
A magnet held above a surface must be repelled by that surface, so look for the statement that describes what happens to the field inside the material.
A

Below its critical temperature a superconductor becomes perfectly diamagnetic and expels magnetic flux from its interior (the Meissner effect). Field lines are bent around the superconductor and a mirror-image repulsion is produced that is strongest directly beneath the magnet, so the magnet is held up. Option A.

content.text: Which row of the table correctly identifies the ring with the greater magnetic flux and the ring with the greater magnetic flux density?
Greater magnetic flux: P.   Greater magnetic flux density: P.
Greater magnetic flux: P.   Greater magnetic flux density: Q.
Greater magnetic flux: Q.   Greater magnetic flux density: P.
Greater magnetic flux: Q.   Greater magnetic flux density: Q.

Magnetic flux is $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$, so it depends on both the field strength and the area. Make the two comparisons separately: which ring sits in the stronger field, and which ring encloses the larger area?
Look carefully at the spacing of the crosses in the two regions. The field is not the same strength in both, and the size of the ring alone does not decide both columns.
C
Two independent comparisons are needed, because $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ contains both $B$ and $A$.

Flux density: the crosses are packed closely together in the region containing ring P and are much further apart in the region containing ring Q, so the field (and hence the flux density $B$) is greater in P's region.
Flux: ring Q encloses a much larger area than ring P, and even though the field there is weaker, the product $B \times A$ is still larger for Q. Ring Q therefore has the greater magnetic flux.

So the correct row is the one giving greater magnetic flux in Q and greater magnetic flux density in P. The rows that give the same ring for both columns fail because the flux density is set by the spacing of the crosses, not by the size of the ring.

content.text: Which physical phenomenon allows current to flow through a metal wire?
Holes can move through a wire.
Charged atoms can move through a wire.
Electrons in a fully filled band can carry charge through a wire.
Electrons in a partially filled band can carry charge through a wire.
A conductor needs empty energy states immediately above the occupied states, so that electrons can move into them when a voltage is applied.
Whole atoms or holes carry charge in semiconductors and ionic conductors, not in a metal wire, and a completely filled band has no empty states beside it.
D

In band theory a metal has a partially filled energy band, so there are unoccupied states infinitesimally above the filled states into which electrons can be excited by an applied voltage. These mobile electrons drift through the wire and carry the charge. A completely filled band has no adjacent empty states available, so it cannot conduct, and charge does not move by whole atoms. Option D.

content.text: Explain the volcanic activity on the island of Hawaii.
Explain how the formation of the Hawaiian island chain can be used as evidence for the theory of plate tectonics.
Start with the ages on the map: which island is the youngest, and where is the volcanic activity concentrated relative to the ends of the chain?
Then use the direction in which the islands become older. That direction is what carries the evidence in the second half of this question, so make the connection between the two explicitly.

items: (c)(i) Hawaii is the youngest island (less than $0.7$ m.y.) and the only island showing current volcanic activity, because it is the only island still positioned over the stationary hot spot. Each new island is formed over the hot spot and is then carried away with the moving Pacific plate, so volcanic activity on an island ceases once it has moved away from the hot spot.

(c)(ii) The islands become progressively older in one consistent direction, in a near-linear relationship with distance from the active south-eastern end of the chain. This is exactly what is expected if a rigid plate moves steadily over a stationary hot spot, so the age pattern is evidence for plate tectonics: it cannot be explained by any process internal to the islands, and it converts a relative observation (age) into a measured rate of plate motion.

content.text: Part (c)(i) is read from the two data sets on the map together: the age annotations, which run from Kauai at $3.8$-$5.6$ m.y. in the north-west to Hawaii at less than $0.7$ m.y. in the south-east, and the key, which shows present-day volcanic activity only on Hawaii. The explanation required is the hot spot model: the most recent island is still over the mantle plume, so it is still being built, while the older islands have been carried away on the moving plate and are now extinct.

Part (c)(ii) needs the pattern rather than the individual ages: age increases steadily with distance from the south-eastern (active) end, and the increase is approximately linear, which corresponds to a constant rate of plate motion. The link to plate tectonics must be made explicitly: an age gradient ordered along the direction of plate motion, centred on a fixed point of volcanism, is a prediction of the theory rather than a local observation. Mentioning the acknowledgement of the source data earns no credit, but citing the direction and the linear trend does.

content.text: How is the orientation of the magnetic axis of a hydrogen nucleus affected by the application of a strong magnetic field during an MRI scan?
Explain the difference in the relaxation time of hydrogen in water and the relaxation time of hydrogen in other molecules.

For the first sub-question, start from what the strong field does to the orientation of each hydrogen nucleus's magnetic moment, given that before the field was applied those moments were pointing in all directions at random.

For the second sub-question, remember that relaxation requires energy to be transferred to the surroundings. It is the rate at which the surrounding molecules tumble, not the nucleus itself, that sets the relaxation time, so ask why water behaves differently from other molecules.

items: (d)(i) With no field applied the hydrogen nuclei are oriented randomly and there is no net magnetisation. A strong field makes each proton's magnetic moment align either parallel (the lower-energy state) or antiparallel (the higher-energy state) to the field, with slightly more nuclei in the parallel state, so a net magnetisation is produced along the direction of the field. The moments also precess about the field direction at the Larmor frequency.

(d)(ii) The relaxation time of hydrogen depends on its molecular environment. In water the molecules tumble very rapidly and transfer energy to the surrounding molecular lattice efficiently, so hydrogen in water has a short relaxation time. Hydrogen in other molecules, such as fat or large organic molecules, is surrounded by molecules that tumble more slowly, so energy transfer is less efficient and the relaxation time is longer. This difference is why different tissues appear with different brightness in an MRI image.

content.text: In (d)(i) the mark is for the individual moments, not just for the sample. Saying the nuclei 'line up with the field' is incomplete because there are two allowed orientations: parallel to the field (lower energy) and antiparallel (higher energy). The full answer states that slightly more occupy the parallel state and therefore a net magnetisation appears along the field, which is what produces the signal later detected.

In (d)(ii) the mark is for the mechanism. Relaxation occurs when hydrogen nuclei transfer energy to their surroundings, and the rate at which that can happen depends on how rapidly the surrounding molecules tumble relative to the precession of the nuclei. Water molecules tumble very rapidly and transfer energy efficiently, giving a short relaxation time; the molecules in other substances tumble more slowly, giving a longer relaxation time. Stating the difference without the mechanism, or without linking it to image contrast, earns only the middle mark.

Measuring the size of the frequency shift gives the component of the blood velocity along the beam, so the flow in an artery or vein can be mapped and areas of blockage, turbulence or reversed flow identified.

A piezoelectric transducer - piezoelectric crystals convert electrical pulses into ultrasound and convert the returning sound waves back into electrical signals, with the same probe used for transmission and reception. 2. Pulse-echo (time-of-flight) technology with a computer - the interval between a transmitted pulse and its echo is converted into the depth of the reflecting structure, and the scanned echoes are assembled by the computer into a two- or three-dimensional image on the monitor.

. With the surface temperature fixed by the spectral class, that relation gives $L \propto R^{2}$, so Matar must be much larger than the Sun in radius, and its luminosity is correspondingly greater. content.text: Describe the transition process of a G2 main sequence star, such as the Sun, evolving into a red giant.
Follow the star forward in time. The first thing that happens is that a fuel is used up, and the question is where and how.

Fusion does not stop everywhere at once. Once the core hydrogen is gone, ask where the fusion moves to, what that does to the layer surrounding the core, and what the increased radiation pressure from that layer does to the envelope above it.
The envelope expanding and cooling changes the star's colour. Name the process that eventually begins abruptly in the core once the envelope has peeled away, and give the name of that event.
Core hydrogen is depleted, the core contracts and heats, shell fusion begins and the envelope expands and cools, then helium fusion ignites in a helium flash.

When a main sequence star such as our sun reaches the end of its life hydrogen in the core is depleted. The nuclear reaction is no longer sustained and the core collapses, heating up the surrounding shell and the core. Hydrogen in the shell will eventually begin to fuse to helium. The surrounding shell expands due to the increased radiation pressure and as it does it cools, becoming more red in colour. The helium fusion reaction in the core will start suddenly and produce a 'helium flash'; the radius of the star will decrease and the star could become unstable and pulsate as a periodic variable.

content.text: The graphs give information that could be used to calculate the distance from Earth to a Type 1 Cepheid Variable.
The star is claimed to be approximately 1260 parsecs from Earth. Show how this claim is supported or refuted by the information in the graphs.
State an advantage and a disadvantage of using the graphs above to calculate the distance to a star.

The period of the light variation of a Cepheid is linked to its true luminosity, so one of the graphs converts a measured period into an absolute magnitude, and the other gives the apparent magnitude as seen from Earth. You then have two magnitudes for the same star, so write down the relation that links apparent magnitude, absolute magnitude and distance before substituting, and note that the distance comes out of it in a form that still has to be evaluated.

Compare the distance you obtain with the claimed 1260 pc and state whether the claim is supported or refuted. Check the size of your answer against the size of the magnitude difference - if the two differ by a factor of ten, look for a misplaced $+5$.
For (ii), keep the two halves separate: an advantage of using these graphs, and a disadvantage of using these graphs. Both are about the method, not about this particular star.
**(i)** $M = -4.0$, $m = 6.5$, so $m - M = 10.5$ and $d = 10^{(m-M+5)/5} = 10^{3.1} = 1.26\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{pc}$. The claim of approximately 1260 parsecs is **supported**.

**(ii)** Advantage: once a Cepheid in a cluster has been measured, the distance to every other member of that cluster follows immediately, and many distances can be obtained far more quickly than by measuring parallax on each star. Disadvantage: the accuracy is limited by the precision of the period measurement and by reading values off two graphs, so the distance carries a large percentage uncertainty, and because bright Cepheids are rare the method is confined to relatively nearby objects.

Step 1 - read the two graphs. The period of the light variation is measured from the observed light curve, and the period-luminosity relation for Type 1 Cepheids converts that period into an absolute magnitude, $M = -4.0$. The second graph gives the apparent magnitude as seen from Earth, $m = 6.5$. The two magnitudes are properties of the same star, which is what makes them comparable.
Step 2 - apply the distance modulus to the difference between the magnitudes.

Step 3 - compare with the claim. $1.26\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{pc} = 1260\,\mathrm{pc}$, so the claim is supported. The two errors that produce a wrong answer here are omitting the $+5$ in the index, which gives $d = 100\,\mathrm{pc}$, and evaluating $10^{3.1}$ as a number close to 10 rather than as $1.26\times10^{3}$.

Part (ii) is a judgement about the method. An advantage is reach: the period-luminosity relation is calibrated on nearby Cepheids whose distances are already known, so the distance to any observable Cepheid, and hence to the cluster or galaxy containing it, follows from a single light curve - something that could not be done for the individual faint members. A disadvantage is accuracy and range: every value in the calculation is read from a graph or from a photon count, so the modulus is only known to about half a magnitude at best, which is a factor of nearly two in distance, and because bright Cepheids are uncommon the method cannot be pushed to great distances, whereas trigonometric parallax, though limited, is exact for the stars it can reach.

Each column of the table needs a different instrument or a different physics principle, so sort the four standard properties into groups before you write anything.

Spectroscopy and photometry are the two workhorses. One of them gives a temperature and a composition by splitting the light into lines; the other gives brightness. Decide which is which, and then think about what extra piece of information is needed to turn brightness into luminosity.

Mass is the difficult one, because a single isolated star cannot be weighed. Recall how the masses of the two stars in a binary system are obtained from the period and separation of their orbit, and which conservation law that relies on.

A spectrograph splits the light into a spectrum compared with known spectra to give composition and temperature; comparison with black body curves gives colour and temperature; photometry and the distance modulus give luminosity; and binary star measurements with Kepler's law give mass.

To determine the characteristics of a star the visible light can be broken up with a spectrograph and then examined. The spectrum is compared to known spectra of other stars. Stars of the A class will have absorption lines showing strong hydrogen lines and ionised metal lines. By comparing the radiation emitted by the star to a black body radiation curve the colour of the star can also be determined as the combination of wavelengths emitted will be white. The temperature of the star can also be determined as stars act as black body radiators and will produce a specific radiation curve at a specific temperature, in this case between 7500 and 10 000 K. The mass of a star can be determined by assuming that stars of the same spectral class and same luminosity class will be the same mass, the standard being produced by determining the mass of a binary star using Kepler's law. The luminosity or absolute magnitude can be determined by using photometry, taking a photo and measuring the magnitude to determine the apparent magnitude and, if the distance to the star is determined, using the distance modulus formula.

content.text: Outline the key features of the Rutherford model of the atom.
Explain how the Bohr model of the atom overcomes an identified limitation of the Rutherford model of the atom.

List what Rutherford kept and what he threw away. The small dense nucleus survived the change of model; the large extended positive charge did not, and the atom is mostly empty space with the electrons far out.

For the second half, name the specific observation the Rutherford model could not reproduce - the observed line spectrum of hydrogen - and then state the single Bohr assumption that removes the difficulty.

Keep the quantisation precise: it is the discrete set of allowed energy levels, and hence the discrete set of emitted photon energies, that does the work. Electrons do not radiate merely because they are accelerating.

items: (i) A small, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom containing nearly all of its mass, with electrons moving around it at a distance; the rest of the atom is empty space.

(ii) The Rutherford model cannot explain the line spectrum of hydrogen, because a charged electron accelerating in an orbit should radiate energy continuously and so produce a continuous spectrum. Bohr restricts the electron to certain allowed orbits with fixed energies and says it radiates only when it moves between them, emitting a single photon of energy $E_i - E_f$. Because the energies are fixed, so are the photon wavelengths, which reproduces the observed discrete lines.

content.text: (i) Rutherford kept the nucleus, which the scattering experiment of Geiger and Marsden had shown to be small, dense and positively charged, and discarded Thomson's diffuse sphere of positive charge, replacing it with electrons in motion around a point-like nucleus. The model therefore has a tiny massive positive core and electrons at a distance from it, so most of the atom's volume is empty space - the alpha-scattering experiment is explained because almost all of the alpha particles pass straight through.

(ii) The identified limitation is the atomic line spectrum. In the Rutherford model an electron in an orbit is a charged particle undergoing centripetal acceleration, so it radiates, and it radiates continuously as it loses energy; that predicts a continuous spectrum, whereas hydrogen and the other elements are observed to emit only a few discrete wavelengths. Bohr's single new postulate is that the electron may occupy only certain allowed orbits, in each of which it has a fixed energy $E_n = -13.6/n^{2}$ eV, and that it radiates only on jumping from one allowed orbit to another. Each jump emits a single photon carrying exactly the difference in energy between the two levels,

so because only certain transitions are possible, only certain photon energies, and hence only certain wavelengths, are produced. The difficulty is removed because the discrete set of energy levels converts the would-be continuous emission into a discrete line spectrum matching what is observed.

The neutrino was suggested to carry away the missing energy and momentum in beta decay, but because it is massless and only weakly interacting it could not be detected, so it was not discovered by Pauli.

content.text: Identify the fundamental forces proposed by the standard model of the atom.
Explain how the stability of atomic nuclei is maintained.
The standard model names four interactions. Remember that gravity is included in the list even though the model does not actually describe it - that is a fair point to make about its limits.

For nuclear stability, set out the competing contributions inside a nucleus: one is enormously strong but acts only over a very short range, the other acts between every pair of protons and grows with their number. Which is which?
Then write the two as an inequality and ask how it changes as the proton number increases. Remember that the protons would not need any help if they were not electrically charged.

items: (i) The electromagnetic, gravitational, strong nuclear and weak nuclear interactions. (The standard model does not actually describe gravity, so it is included here as the fourth fundamental force even though it lies outside the model.)

(ii) Nuclei are held together by the attractive strong nuclear force between nucleons, which acts over a range of only about $10^{-15}\,\mathrm{m}$ but is strong enough to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between every pair of protons. Because the repulsive Coulomb force grows with the number of protons while the attractive nuclear force saturates, stability requires more neutrons than protons as the nucleus gets heavier, since neutrons add binding without adding repulsion - which is why stable nuclei have a neutron-to-proton ratio of about 1:1 when light, rising to about 1.5:1 for the heaviest nuclei.

content.text: (i) Four fundamental interactions account for all known behaviour of matter at the atomic and nuclear scale: the electromagnetic force between charged particles, the weak nuclear force responsible for beta decay, the strong nuclear force that binds the nucleus, and gravity. Particles in the standard model are quarks and leptons, and each of the first three interactions is mediated by exchange particles (photons, W and Z bosons and gluons respectively).

(ii) Two forces act between the nucleons in a nucleus. The electromagnetic force is repulsive between each pair of protons, and because the nucleus as a whole is charged, the total repulsive force grows roughly with the square of the proton number. The strong nuclear force is attractive, and although it is enormously strong per pair it is short-ranged, so each nucleon interacts strongly only with its immediate neighbours and its contribution saturates. For small numbers of protons the attractive term dominates and the nucleus is stable without any correction. As the proton number rises, the repulsive term grows and eventually the nucleus would fly apart, so extra neutrons are needed to raise the total number of strong-force pairs without adding any electrostatic repulsion. This is why the neutron-to-proton ratio in stable nuclei climbs from about 1:1 for light nuclei to about 1.5:1 for the heaviest, and why nuclei above that ratio, and all nuclei above $Z \approx 83$, are unstable and decay.

De Broglie extended the particle model of light to matter, showing that electrons have wave properties, which explained the quantised energy levels of the atom and wave-particle duality.

De Broglie was able to utilise the current understanding of matter to further develop our understanding of the structure of matter. At the time there was an understanding of the nature of light, which was energy displaying particle-like properties. Also, a model of the atom was established displaying quantised electron energy levels, but this was yet to be explained. content.text: Describe an ideal operational amplifier.
Start with the ideal properties themselves. There are four of them that matter, and one of them - the resistance looking into the inputs - is the reason the rest of the circuit becomes simple.

For (ii), decide first where the signal must go and where the feedback must go. An inverting amplifier sends the input to one particular input terminal and returns a fraction of the output to that same terminal, so draw the feedback path and work backwards to the resistance needed.

For (iii), the gain of an inverting amplifier is negative. Treat the magnitude and the sign as two separate pieces of information: one of them fixes the height of your sketch, the other decides whether crests stay crests or become troughs.

** An ideal operational amplifier reproduces its input signal at the output with only the voltage changed: it has **infinite input resistance**, so no current flows into either input and the two inputs are at the same potential whenever the output is not saturated; **zero output resistance**, so the output voltage is unaffected by the load connected to it; and **infinite open-loop gain** with **infinite bandwidth**, so even a tiny difference between the two input voltages drives the output to one of the supply rails, with no limit on the frequency range. In use with negative feedback the output is a faithful, amplified reproduction of the input signal, larger in voltage only.
**

The first is the one that makes the rest easy: because no current flows into either input, the input circuit does not load the signal source, and the two inputs are at the same potential to an accuracy set only by how large the open-loop gain is. Infinite gain means that in practice the output is always driven to one of the supply rails unless feedback is used to hold it back.

The physical limit to watch is the size of an atom itself. Once a transistor is only a few atoms across, quantum effects such as tunnelling between neighbouring channels become significant and the device stops behaving classically.

Integrated circuits, microprocessors and multiple core processors have packed more transistors into less space and used less power, meeting society's increasing computing needs, although quantum effects now limit further miniaturisation and dependence on technology creates new risks.

Early computers each employed hundreds of thousands of single transistors. However, as the need for faster, more powerful and lightweight computers arose, scientists had to work out a way of packing more transistors into a small space. This led to the integrated circuit, which contained millions of transistors on a single chip. This uses far less power and takes up far less space for a given processing ability. As computing needs increase, more and more transistors are placed onto a single chip. This means they become closer and closer to physical limits due to the size of atoms and so quantum effects become significant, where electrons tunnel across the transistors and interfere with one another. Portable computers now make use of multiple core processors working in parallel to increase computing power rather than further miniaturisation of the chip. Society now has access to smaller and more powerful computers, increasing productivity and communication worldwide, though there are also negative impacts as people become over-reliant on the technology.
